title: Does an Executable Generate–Validate–Repair Loop Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM-Generated NetOps Changes?
abstract: We report a preregistered, paired experiment comparing an executable generate→validate→repair pipeline (guarded) against an LLM-only suggestion workflow (baseline) for intent-driven network-configuration tasks. The confirmatory design used N=120 paired intent→configuration tasks executed against a deterministic emulator-based validator; all candidate configurations were produced by a single hosted LLM (gpt-5-mini) under a frozen prompting/configuration plan. The preregistered primary estimand was the paired reduction in emulator-observed semantic failures. All 120 paired observations produced emulator-valid configurations in both conditions (baseline success rate = 1.00; guarded success rate = 1.00), yielding a paired-difference estimate = 0.00 (exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00], bootstrap resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). We incorporate reviewer-requested clarifications grounded in archived execution artifacts: (i) the run used a single shared initial generation per task (one model call per task) to isolate validator/repair effects and thereby explains model_calls_used=120 despite a planned maximum of 240; (ii) repair logic triggered only when the emulator reported violations (no guarded repairs were applied: repair_applied=false for all guarded episodes); and (iii) key artifact hashes for preregistration, raw results, model configuration, paired-contingency table, and analysis log are reported to allow direct artifact lookup. We conclude that, for this curated synthetic task bank, model, and frozen prompting/configuration, the guarded loop did not change semantic-outcome rates; we discuss ceiling effects, external-validity limits, and paths for follow-up evaluations.

sections.introduction: Automating NetOps tasks with LLMs promises productivity but raises safety and correctness concerns: syntactically plausible configurations can still violate workflow or protocol constraints and cause semantic regressions. Prior work therefore recommends tool-augmented pipelines—generate→validate→repair—or constraining LLMs to translation roles paired with verified solvers to reduce operational risk. To provide a preregistered, artifact-backed test of these recommendations, we asked: Does inserting an executable emulator-based validator into a generate→validate→repair loop reduce semantic/network-level failures of LLM-generated configuration changes compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow? We preregistered study CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1, implemented a deterministic emulator validator and task generator, and executed a paired experiment over N=120 tasks using a single hosted LLM (gpt-5-mini). Our contributions: (1) a preregistered paired confirmatory experiment with deterministic artifacts; (2) explicit, artifact-grounded clarifications requested by peer review (shared-generation semantics, repair-trigger logic, and artifact-hash table); and (3) a transparent discussion of a null/ceiling confirmatory result and its implications for broader NetOps evaluation.
sections.related_work: Surveys and benchmarks that execute LLM outputs in emulation or formal verification reveal semantic failure modes that syntax-only evaluation misses and motivate verifier-augmented workflows. Recent executable-benchmark efforts and tool-augmented agent architectures (generate→validate→repair, veto layers, canaries, digital twins) report improved detection/prevention of semantic errors in controlled settings, though comparisons vary in task scope, model diversity, and validator fidelity. Our study is positioned as a preregistered, reproducible confirmatory test: it does not attempt to replace those broader evaluations but rather to assess a guarded loop’s efficacy under a precisely specified, deterministic harness and a fixed single-model configuration.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: We preregistered CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1 before execution. The design: paired binary comparison over 120 distinct intent→configuration tasks; each task produced two episodes—baseline (LLM-only suggestion applied to emulator) and guarded (same LLM suggestion subjected to generate→validate→repair pipeline that could issue at most one repair iteration). Analysis: primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, tested with exact two-sided McNemar; alpha=0.05; bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10k resamples, seed=1729. Model and prompt: all candidate configurations were produced by gpt-5-mini under a frozen prompt and adapter settings recorded pre-run (see model_configuration.json). Shared-initial-generation semantics and model-call accounting: the preregistered execution_contract allowed a shared initial generation per paired task (shared_initial_generation). We intentionally used a single shared initial generation per task (initial_generation_calls_per_task=1, independent_condition_generation=false in the preregistration) so baseline and guarded conditions compared the same LLM candidate rather than conflating generation variance with validator/repair effects. This explains model_calls_used=120 despite a planned maximum of 240. Repair-trigger logic and repair budget: the guarded pipeline attempted a single repair iteration only if the deterministic emulator validator reported violation_count>0 on the initial candidate; preregistered maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1. In this run, validator traces record repair_applied=false for every guarded episode (no repairs were invoked or applied). Execution harness and determinism: a deterministic emulator-based validator executed and checked candidate configurations against task-specific intent constraints and workflow policies (e.g., make-before-break, shutdown→change→restore). Inclusion/exclusion and missingness: technical/infrastructure failures would be excluded per the preregistration; none occurred. Artifact-hash table (key archived artifacts): preregistration manifest SHA-256 = 0bfc96e9afceed579f04a06dcbad2387ee4acca970559d9a4faa165893f4fe50; execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA-256 = ad350dd7a4350630a2ff9126f86a9a19e61a714e5bda1b8c1591862da769be2a; execution/model_configuration.json SHA-256 = 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa; analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA-256 = 9f25790c7eeaafb3562e0710e0cf10b7a47a55ea00fcbcf02eee324f79afafe7; analysis/analysis_log.jsonl SHA-256 = 82803fc5d3e9722c78c7d3149136de35c3c04c5d69b8abb43b39f98fb50a839b. Representative provider-call and response artifacts (shared-generation traces) are provided in execution/provider_calls/* and execution/responses/* (see the archived manifest and the representative hashes in the evidence bundle).
sections.results: Execution accounting: the run completed per the preregistered plan (execution manifest). All planned episodes completed: 240 episodes (120 pairs); model_calls_used = 120 (one shared initial generation per task). Validator scoring: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 reported valid configurations for every episode. Contingency table: n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0 (all pairs concordant successful). Observed success rates: baseline = 120/120 = 1.00; guarded = 120/120 = 1.00. Confirmatory test: paired-difference estimate = 0.00; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10k resamples, seed = 1729). Repair activity: per the archived validator traces and scoring JSON files (execution/scoring/*.json), repair_applied = false for every guarded episode; the guarded repair stage was never invoked because the validator reported violation_count = 0 on all initial candidates. Secondary outcomes: preregistered secondary metrics (mean model calls per successful task; count of tasks requiring repair) are vacuous here: no repairs were applied and model calls per task reflect the single shared generation design. Missingness and contamination: no episodes were excluded; contamination detectors in the manifest report no flags.
sections.discussion: Interpretation and ceiling effect: the confirmatory result is a null effect: on this curated synthetic task bank and deterministic harness, the guarded generate→validate→repair loop did not reduce semantic failures because the baseline already produced emulator-valid configurations for all tasks. This outcome is an artifact of the joint execution conditions (task generator, model, frozen prompt, and validator). Importantly, because baseline success reached 100%, the preregistered target effect (absolute reduction of 0.15) and power assumptions do not apply—the observed ceiling renders the McNemar test vacuous for demonstrating the intended reduction. We therefore treat the result as an artifact-backed narrow null: it shows that under these controlled conditions a guarded loop produced no additional benefit, not that guarded or verifier-augmented designs are generally unnecessary. Design choices and reproducibility tradeoffs: the shared-initial-generation choice (one LLM call per task, shared between conditions) was deliberate to isolate validator/repair efficacy from generation variability; reviewers requested this explicit justification and the artifact traces demonstrating the shared provider calls are cited above. Limitations that constrain generalization (single-model, frozen prompting, synthetic task bank, deterministic emulator fidelity) are discussed below and must guide interpretation. Operational implications: a guarded loop remains a defensible safety architecture in more heterogeneous, noisy, or adversarial production settings (consistent with prior work); our findings emphasize the need for diverse task banks, multi-model studies, richer repair budgets, and higher-fidelity validators to evaluate the operational value of guarded workflows in the wild.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=120 tasks) comparing an emulator-validated generate→validate→repair pipeline to an LLM-only workflow using a deterministic harness and a single hosted LLM (gpt-5-mini). All paired episodes were emulator-valid in both conditions (n_11=120), yielding a paired difference of 0.00 (exact McNemar p = 1.0). Reviewer-requested clarifications derived from archived artifacts are incorporated: the run used a shared initial generation per task (explaining model_calls_used=120), repair attempts were conditional on validator-detected violations (none occurred; repair_applied=false across guarded episodes), and key artifact hashes are listed for direct lookup. The result is narrowly scoped: a ceiling effect on a synthetic, well-scoped task bank under a frozen prompt/model configuration. Follow-up studies should use production-rooted incident corpora, multiple models/prompts, larger repair budgets, and higher-fidelity or multi-vendor validators to assess guarded-loop benefits under operational heterogeneity. All execution and analysis artifacts referenced here are archived per the preregistration and manifest for reproducibility and inspection.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), a frozen prompting strategy, and a deterministic emulator validator; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.

Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is therefore constrained.

Single-model, single-prompt budget: only one model and a single shared-generation budget per task were evaluated; multi-model ensembles, alternative prompts, or higher-budget multi-iteration repair regimes were not tested.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but necessarily simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, producing a ceiling effect that violates the preregistered power assumptions (targeted 0.15 absolute reduction) and renders the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for detecting the prespecified effect size.
